title: Practice in meetings
hookLine: listening, patience, and not needing to win

cards: Someone is speaking. Around the table, or across a grid of small faces on a screen, people nod. Some are listening.
Some are rehearsing the clever thing they'll say the moment there's a gap. One has the camera off and is answering email. The speaker finishes, and three people start talking at once.
Nobody meant any harm. A meeting just has a way of turning into a contest without anyone deciding it should. Old texts about speech and silence speak to that room.

teach.h: SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO SPEAK.
teach.b: First, the letter of James, in the King James Bible: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath."
Hearing comes first, and it's the only one of the three meant to be quick. Speaking waits. Anger waits too.
Second, Proverbs names the opposite: "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him."
That's the reply that starts before the question is finished, ready because it was never really listening. Third, a tradition with a way of meeting.
In a Quaker meeting for business, among the Religious Society of Friends, decisions are made without a vote.
Friends speak, they listen, they sit in silence, and they seek what Friends call the sense of the meeting. It can be slow.
It's built on the idea that the answer may come from anyone in the room, including someone quiet in the corner.
Fourth, not needing to win. The Tao Te Ching, in its twenty-second chapter, says that because the sage does not strive, no one in the world can strive with him.
In a meeting that looks plain: letting someone finish a sentence, asking a real question instead of making a point, letting a good idea be someone else's.
Listening isn't agreeing. It's letting a person be fully heard before you answer. A simple test helps: before speaking, could you say back what the last person meant, in a way they'd recognize?
If not, the turn to speak can wait one more breath.

how: Quakers hold meetings for business in which decisions are reached without a vote, by seeking the sense of the meeting; Christians read James 1:19 as a rule for everyday speech.

games.q: what's inside listening in the room — tap the pairs.
p: swift to hear, slow to speak

s: James says to be swift to speak and slow to hear
it's the other way round: swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.
Quaker meetings for business decide without voting
Friends listen, keep silence and seek the sense of the meeting.
Proverbs praises the quick answer given before the question is done
answering before hearing, it says, is folly and shame unto him.

games.q: you're in a Quaker meeting for business, and the room is divided. what do Friends do instead of taking a vote?
o: listen, keep silence and seek the sense of the meeting.
put it off until everyone gives up.
games.why: they seek the sense of the meeting, on the idea that the answer may come from anyone in the room.

practice: Picture your next meeting, or a conversation at home that tends to turn into a contest, and the person who most often frustrates you there.
Imagine letting them finish every sentence, and when the urge to prepare your reply comes, set it down the way you'd set down a cup.
Then find one real question you could ask them instead of a point to make; if you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words.
